title: MC0-09013
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (female appellant) and XXXX XXXX (male appellant) are citizens of Algeria. They are accompanied by their minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (minor appellants), who are citizens of Algeria.

The female appellant fears her father and her in-laws. The family lives with the male appellant's father. She explains that she is mistreated there and that they want her to wear a hijab. The male appellant also fears his father and his father-in-law.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) concluded that the appellants were not credible because of contradictions, omissions and inconsistencies between the testimony and the Basis of Claim Forms (BOC Forms).
The appellants are alleging that the RPD erred in its analysis of their credibility.

The determinative issue for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is whether the RPD erred in its analysis of the male appellant's credibility and its analysis of the female appellant's claim under section 96 on a Convention ground.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD correctly determined that the male appellant, XXXX XXXX, is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

I allow the appeal. The RPD erred. The files of XXXX XXXX and the children, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX are referred to a differently constituted panel of the RPD with directions.

My role is to examine all of the evidence, which includes reading the transcript and listening to the hearing, and to determine whether the RPD's decision is correct.1 The male appellant did not establish the allegations in his refugee protection claim

The male appellant alleges that he fears his father, who does not accept his behaviour as a non-practising Muslim, and his father-in-law, who does not accept his daughter's marriage. The male appellant's claim must therefore be assessed under section 96 on the ground of religion and from the perspective of section 97.

The male appellant's allegations are as follows: in his BOC Form, he explains that he fears his wife's father (XXXX XXXX XXXX) and his own family (XXXX family). It is alleged that XXXX XXXX XXXX threatened to take him to court if he refused to divorce and never left him alone. It is alleged that the XXXX family forced his wife to wear a hijab. In a paragraph addressing the threats from both families, he adds that his children suffered and were harassed, without specifying who is behind this fear. In response to question 2(h) in the BOC Form, he states that the children were bullied at school.

At the hearing, when the RPD asked him what he fears, the male appellant spontaneously described his fear of his father, who forced his wife to wear a hijab. He added that his father has been causing problems for him since he was XXXX years old and that the conflict stems from the fact that he is a non-practising Muslim. Later, when the RPD pointed out to him that he does not make these allegations in his BOC Form, he explained that he had problems with [translation] "the missus's father," who allegedly wanted him to divorce his daughter and who did not want his daughter to wear a hijab. The male appellant omitted the allegations against his father from his Basis of Claim Form

The RPD considered that the male appellant's testimony contradicted the information in the BOC Form concerning the identity of the persecutor. It noted that, at the hearing, the male appellant explained that he feared his father, whereas in his BOC Form, he mentions fearing his father-in-law, and that in his BOC Form, the male appellant does not explain that his father's treatment is due to the fact that he is a non-practising Muslim. It considered that, in light of the sudden addition of these new statements and the confusion they caused, the male appellant's testimony was not credible. The RPD did not accept the explanations that he did not mention his father-in-law because the RPD did not ask about him. The RPD drew a negative influence regarding the male appellant's credibility.

The appellants argue that the RPD erred in its interpretation of the facts and that it considered that the male appellant is the principal claimant, when it is the female appellant, which led to confusion, and that the persecutor is in fact the father-in-law. They consider that submitting additional information actually corroborates the content of the BOC Form and that they had no intention to mislead the RPD.

The RPD did not err in its interpretation of the facts. Joint refugee protection claims are analyzed on an individual basis. The fact that one of the claimants is considered the principal must not impact the analysis of the other's claim. In this case, the appellants' allegations set out in paragraph 2 of their respective BOC Forms are different and personalized. The children's BOC Forms are based on the parents' written accounts. Moreover, the male appellant indicates in his IMM5669 form that he is the principal applicant, which contradicts his statement in his memorandum that he is the associate claimant.
The RPD's conclusion is correct. The male appellant's credibility is undermined by the significant, if not critical omission from his original BOC Form that his father is his agent of persecution.

In his BOC Form, he does not mention his father at all. In response to question 2(a) in the BOC Form, he states, [translation] "I have been threatened by my wife's father, who wants to destroy my family, and by my own family, who force my wife to wear a hijab, and I am afraid that all of this pressure will aggravate the condition of my wife, who has high blood pressure, and this has been very difficult for my children." In response to question 2(b), he does not mention his father, nor does he do so in response to questions 2(c) through 2(h). In response to question 2(h), he reiterates that his family forces his wife to wear a hijab, without any mention of his father.

In his BOC Form, the male appellant mentions only his family, and the alleged fear is not for him, but rather for his wife, in that his family forces her to wear a hijab against her will. When refugee protection claimants complete their BOC Forms, they must include everything that is important for their claims; the claim form states this clearly in capital letters. He took a risk in not disclosing in his initial written account all of the facts and details that are important to a claim for refugee protection.2

The fear of his father is significant, if not critical. It is based on religious grounds and thus changes the basis for the refugee protection claim. At the hearing, the male appellant explained that since the age of XXXX, he has been in conflict with his father, who does not accept that he is a non-practising Muslim or that he drinks alcohol. Based on these new allegations, the male appellant's fear takes on a religious component, a Convention ground, whereas no religious grounds affecting him directly are mentioned in his BOC Form, other than with respect to his wife and wearing a hijab. These new allegations also add a new agent of persecution to the male appellant's claim because, according to the BOC Form, the only person he fears is his wife's father. He mentions his family, but not that he fears them. The fear is instead for his wife.

The male appellant made no mention of this omission before or at the start of the hearing. However, when he signed his BOC Form, he was accompanied by the same counsel as at the hearing, as evidenced by counsel's signature. I do not accept his explanations that the forms were not verified prior to the hearing or that it is because the forms were completed at an Internet cafÚ. When he signed his BOC Form, he declared that the information in the form was complete, true and correct, which he also stated at the hearing. The male appellant also knew that it was possible to amend a claim at the start of the hearing, since the appellants amended the BOC Form to add the recent death of the female appellant's mother. Despite this, the male appellant did not make any amendment to his BOC Form in relation to his fear of his father.

The male appellant is responsible for ensuring that the information in his refugee protection claim is correct. Refugee protection claimants may explain certain aspects of their stories, add details or clarify the evidence in amended versions of their BOC Forms or even at the hearing. However, when these [translation] "clarifications" are central to the claim and are omitted from the original BOC Form, the RPD may draw a negative inference as to the claimant's credibility.

The male appellant never mentions in his BOC Form that he fears his father. This omission is a critical element of his refugee protection claim and undermines his credibility concerning his fear of his father. The male appellant's behaviour in continuing to live in his father's home undermines his credibility

The RPD considered that the appellants' behaviour was inconsistent with their fear of the male appellant's father, given that the appellants always lived in the home of the male appellant's father despite the difficulties alleged. It drew a negative inference regarding the male appellant's credibility. The RPD did not accept the male appellant's explanation that he had nowhere else to go and could not afford to live elsewhere, particularly since he paid his father to live in his home. The RPD was of the opinion that the fact that they relocated briefly to Tizi Ouzou demonstrated that they could afford to rent housing.
The appellants are not specifically challenging this conclusion.

The RPD's conclusion is correct. By remaining in the home of the male appellant's father despite their alleged fear, the appellants, particularly the male appellant, exhibited behaviour that is inconsistent with their fear.

The assessment of the subjective fear (or inconsistent behaviour) is based on certain behaviours considered to be inconsistent with this type of fear. That said, in his BOC Form and at the hearing, the male appellant explained clearly that he continued living with his father from 2008 to 2018 for economic reasons, which is corroborated by the certificate of accommodation signed by his father and filed on the RPD record. In this statement, the father, the alleged agent of persecution, confirms that the male appellant is married, has three children and has lived with him since birth in the XXXX district of Algiers. At the hearing, the male appellant explained that he continued living with his father for economic reasons. However, he also explained that he was working, since he is now receiving a pension. He testified further that he was paying his father money toward certain expenses. I do not accept his explanation. He could have taken his family to live elsewhere if he feared his father rather than remaining, for 10 years, in the home of the person he alleges is his persecutor. The fact that the male appellant stayed in his father's home for 10 years when he states that he was persecuted by him undermines his credibility.

I consider that the female appellant continued living with her in-laws because, based on the documentary evidence, she had no choice but to follow her husband.3 However, the question was not put to her directly by the RPD. I refer to my specific analysis of her claim later in these reasons.

The RPD could make a negative finding as to the male appellant's credibility based on the omission from his BOC Form of his father being the agent of persecution. This omission regarding an important element of the male appellant's claim, namely, that his father was threatening him because he was non-practising, and the fact that he continued to live in his father's home for 10 years compounds this lack of credibility of the male appellant's allegations. He did not establish the risk in relation to his father. The appellants did not establish that they relocated to Tizi Ouzou

The RPD considers that the male appellant contradicted the information in his BOC Form to the effect that he never moved to another part of the country. When the RPD asked him why he had never moved, he explained that he had left for Tizi Ouzou in XXXX 2011 with his family. When the RPD confronted him with this contradiction, the male appellant did not provide any explanation and instead adjusted his testimony by explaining that, for 10 days, he tried to relocate to Tizi Ouzou, but that they had to return to his father's home due to problems his father had caused. The RPD was of the view that his explanation was not satisfactory and that if the male appellant had made a genuine effort to leave his father's home, this would have been indicated clearly in his BOC Form. It added that this contradiction and omission undermined the male appellant's credibility.

The RPD's conclusion is correct. The male appellant makes no mention of his attempt to move to Tizi Ouzou in either his BOC Form or his form upon entering Canada. In his BOC Form, the male appellant indicates in response to question 2(d) that he never moved because he could not afford to rent an apartment or feed his children and that he managed to get by on food donated by neighbours but that it was not enough.

The fact that the male appellant attempted to move out of his father's home is important. At the hearing, he explained that this attempt had failed because his uncles had informed his father that he was in Tizi Ouzou. This information is relevant to the analysis of the capacity of the alleged agent of persecution to locate the male appellant if he attempted to relocate. As I explained earlier in these reasons, the male appellant was required to provide all important information in his BOC Form. The RPD could expect him to do so because he was accompanied by counsel from the time he signed his BOC Form. He did not amend his BOC Form either before or at the start of the hearing and did in fact confirm that all information in his BOC Form was complete and correct, both at the time of signing the BOC Form and at the hearing. The omission of his relocation to Tizi Ouzou is not determinative in itself; however, it undermines the male appellant's credibility when analyzed cumulatively with the omission of his alleged fear of his father. The male appellant did not establish that he relocated to Tizi Ouzou in 2011. The male appellant did not establish the risk in respect of his father-in-law

The RPD noted that the male appellant states in his BOC Form that he cannot afford to pay a lawyer to defend himself against the female appellant's father's threats, yet he submitted in evidence a letter from a lawyer. The RPD did not accept the two appellants' explanations whereby the female appellant stated that she had not thought to add it and that it was her mother who insisted on lending him money because she knew how stubborn her husband was being toward the male appellant.

The appellants submit that the RPD failed to take into account the harm and the threats to which the male appellant was subjected because of his father-in-law or to explain why it rejected the evidence.

The appellants are correct. The RPD did not draw any specific conclusions in relation to fearing XXXX XXXX XXXX. I will therefore respond to this argument. I consider that this issue of assessing the male appellant's risk in respect of his father-in-law is not a new issue for the RAD since it was raised by the appellants.

In his BOC Form, the male appellant alleges that his father-in-law wants to destroy his family, that he threatens to fabricate a story and take him to court if he does not divorce, and that he does not leave him alone. The male appellant argues that he cannot take legal action against his father-in-law because he cannot afford a lawyer and because taking action against one's family is something that people do not do in his community.

He reiterated these allegations at the hearing. The female appellant added that taking action against one's father or father-in-law is something that people do not do and that they could be killed for doing so.

The fact that his father-in-law is threatening to take the male appellant to court is neither a threat nor a risk to the male appellant's life. Although the male appellant explained that there is a risk of being killed if one takes legal action against one's in-laws, nothing in the documentary evidence supports this conclusion, whether the evidence in the National Documentation Package or the evidence provided by the appellants. The male appellant did not allege that his father-in-law made death threats against him or attacked him. The male appellant also stated at the hearing that the person he feared most was his father, not his father-in-law. The letter from the lawyer consulted by the female appellant does not change my analysis, since this letter discusses the female appellant's problems with her father, not those of her husband.
The male appellant did not establish the risk in relation to his father-in-law. The appellants omitted the names of several family members from their Basis of Claim Forms

The RPD noted that both adult appellants neglected to include the names of several members of their respective families in their forms. The female appellant explained that her husband had been the one who completed the forms at an Internet cafÚ. The male appellant explained that the person who filled in the information did not understand what he was telling him. The RPD considered that the appellants had ample opportunity to make any corrections to the forms. In the RPD's view, the appellants had had the same counsel from the start and they confirmed that the content of their BOC Forms was complete, true and correct. The RPD found that the appellants' credibility was called into question because the content of their documentation was incomplete and inaccurate.

The appellants argue that they did not have an opportunity to clarify these contradictions, that the RPD failed to consider the fact that the male appellant completed the forms while he was in Algeria with someone working at an Internet cafÚ who was not a professional, and that these individuals are public letter-writers who provide a service for completing forms for people who are illiterate. They consider that the RPD erred in stating that they had had the same counsel since initiating their refugee protection claims, when the recording of the hearing indicates that they explained to the member that they had never met with a lawyer before submitting their forms. The appellants state that they never realized that information was missing from their forms and that their counsel explained that she had never verified them. The appellants believe that they answered all of the RPD's questions, that their testimony was credible and that they did not conceal anything. They state that they mentioned all of their brothers and sisters and had no interest in concealing their existence, and that if they had wanted to conceal their existence, they would have done so at the hearing, especially since their brothers and sisters are not mentioned in any documents on the record.

The RPD's conclusion is correct. The appellants omitted several brothers and sisters from their BOC Forms. The appellants amended their respective BOC Forms at the start of the hearing to each add brothers and sisters they had neglected to list in their BOC Forms. They had the opportunity to explain these omissions at the hearing.

I note that both of them listed their family members under lines (a) through (k) based on the space limitations of the form. They should have added the other family members on a separate page starting at line (l). Refugee protection claims must be complete and must include the names of parents, children, and brothers and sisters, including half-brothers and half-sisters. This is clearly indicated in the form. The fact that the appellants completed the forms at an Internet cafÚ does not explain the omission, given that when they signed their BOC Forms on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, they were assisted by counsel, as their signatures on the forms confirm. The RPD could expect the forms to have been properly completed.

These omissions do not undermine their credibility, notably because the brothers' and sisters' names are not central to either the female appellant's or the male appellant's refugee protection claims. Credibility findings concerning the male appellant

The RPD's conclusion is correct. The male appellant is not credible. He did not establish the risk in relation to his father because this fear, which is central to his claim, was omitted from his BOC Form and because his behaviour is inconsistent with his fear, in that he continued living with his father, the alleged agent of persecution. He did not establish that he attempted to relocate to Tizi Ouzou because said relocation was omitted from his BOC Form, nor did he establish the risk in relation to his father-in-law. The female appellant's refugee protection claim

The female appellant alleges that she fears her father and her in-laws. According to her BOC Form, she fears her in-laws because they want to force her to wear a hijab. At the hearing, she added that they did not leave her alone and that her brothers-in-law and sisters-in-law who lived with them [translation] "always find something to say about my behaviour." She explained that the harassment she was subjected to is based on religious grounds. She also fears her father, who does not accept her marriage. In view of the allegations, I consider that the female appellant's claim must be analyzed under section 96 on two Convention grounds: religion and gender. I applied the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution (Guideline) in analyzing the female appellant's refugee protection claim. Contradiction regarding the female appellant's address

The RPD noted that the female appellant contradicted herself at the hearing with respect to her home address. She testified that she had been living at her in-laws' home with her husband and her children since 2008, whereas the address she indicates in her form is different from that of her husband. The female appellant explained that she had indicated her parents' address in her form, that she had not known why it was indicated as such, and that her husband had been the one who completed the forms. The RPD considered that the female appellant did not provide satisfactory explanations and that her credibility was undermined by the fact that she had been living with her in-laws since 2008.

The RPD's conclusion is correct. In his IMM5669 form, the male appellant gives only one address, in the XXXX district of Algiers. The female appellant, meanwhile, gives another address, in the XXXX XXXX district of Algiers. At the hearing, the female appellant stated that she lived at her father-in-law's home in XXXX.4 When the RPD returned to the issue of the addresses, the female appellant explained that she had indicated her parents' address in her form but did not know why.5

The contradiction regarding the female appellant's address in her BOC Form is significant because her place of residence is the reason why she fears her in-laws. This contradiction raises a credibility issue. The contradiction concerning the threat from the female appellant's father

The RPD considered that the female appellant contradicted herself concerning her father's threat to take her children away from her. In the BOC Form, she states that she fears that her father will take away her children if she refuses to divorce, whereas at the hearing, she stated instead that she would be able to go back to living at her father's home, but not her children. The RPD did not accept the female appellant's explanations that she believed that her father was using her children to blackmail her. It added that the male appellant testified that his father-in-law was threatening to take his daughter and children from him, whereas he testified that in the event of divorce the female appellant would be responsible for the children. The RPD considered that the female appellant attempted to mislead it and drew a negative inference as to her credibility regarding the father's threats to take her children away from her.

The RPD was correct in concluding that there was a contradiction between the female appellant's BOC Form and her testimony at the hearing. In her BOC Form, the female appellant states that she fears that her father will take her children away from her if she does not divorce her husband. At the hearing, the male appellant testified that XXXX XXXX XXXX wanted to take away the children if his daughter did not divorce. Meanwhile, the female appellant testified that if she divorced, she would be able to return to her parents' home, but that her father would not take in the children because he would not agree to raising a stranger's children. When the RPD confronted her with this contradiction between her BOC Form and her testimony, she explained that her father threatened to take her children away from her and that this was what she feared. This contradiction raises a credibility issue. Analysis under section 96 and the failure to apply the Guideline

The RPD erred in failing to apply the Guideline. Although gender-related fear is not raised explicitly by the appellants and they did not submit this issue before the RAD, to address this issue, I must conduct my analysis in light of the Guideline, since I consider that the female appellant's fear is based on a Convention ground, the fact that she is a woman.

According to the Guideline, the definition of Convention refugee can be interpreted as offering protection to women who demonstrate that they have a well-founded fear of gender-related persecution based on one of the grounds set out in section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. The refugee protection claimant's testimony is then assessed from the perspective of a woman who is from a country where the cultural standards are different for women and where women find themselves in vulnerable situations. Although the Guideline does not have the force of law and is not binding, it defines an appropriate framework, and failure to apply it in appropriate cases may constitute a reviewable error,6 as in the female appellant's case.

In keeping with the Guideline, when assessing whether the female appellant's claim is credible and trustworthy, I must take into account certain difficulties that can arise due to cultural differences. That said, according to the documentary evidence,7 cultural differences exist in Algeria regarding the rights of women; in particular, women must generally reside with their husbands or members of their extended family, such as parents or siblings. The Guideline also instructs me to take into account the fact that some women may be reluctant to testify concerning their situation in certain situations.

In this case, the female appellant alleges in her BOC Form that she fears her in-laws, who forced her to wear a hijab. She adds that she had no choice because she lived with them. She explains that on several occasions, in 2009, 2012 and 2014, her in-laws threw her out of the house for refusing to wear a hijab, after which she decided to wear one because she had no choice in order to protect her children.

At the hearing, she added that her children must wear djellabas against her will and that if she protests she could be killed. She stated that she did not have the right to speak or to work and that the father-in-law does not leave her alone and is always standing over her, because she lives in the same house. Her brothers-in-law spit on her because they are practising and do not consider her to be a proper woman. However, she claimed that, despite all of these problems, she had been living with her in-laws for 10 years, with her husband staying in his parents' home in order to protect her. He stated at the hearing that he had no choice as he did not have enough money. The male appellant took no measures to protect his wife from the fear she has of the XXXX family, despite stating in his BOC Form and testifying at the hearing that it has made his wife sick. The RPD never asked the female appellant whether she had the option of living elsewhere.

In order to assess the female appellant's claim under section 96 on the ground of a fear of gender-related persecution, I must determine whether the harm suffered by the female appellant is a form of persecution. The fact that the RPD did not consider the female appellant's claim from this perspective meant that the RPD asked few questions concerning the female appellant's situation, in terms of her situation as a woman and her marital situation. It also did not question her about her right to work, nor did it ask her to provide details about the harassment she experienced while living in her father-in-law's home with the brothers-in-law and sisters-in-law.

In addition, I consider that the female appellant was subjected to harm based on the fact that she testified, in her husband's presence, about allegations involving his family and the actions of her husband, who failed to protect her. She was also subjected to harm based on the fact that, as she stated at the hearing, XXXX XXXX XXXX was the one who completed the forms himself at the Internet cafÚ.

Although they raise certain credibility issues, the contradictions regarding the female appellant's address and her fear of her father are insufficient to conclude that the female appellant is not credible.

For these reasons, I cannot determine whether her fear is well-founded; specifically, I do not have sufficient evidence to determine the objective basis of her claim under section 96. The female appellant's vulnerability as an Algerian woman whose husband is asking her to live in his father's home even though she alleges to fear her in-laws is central to her refugee protection claim. However, this does not mean that I have sufficient evidence to establish that she is a Convention refugee, due to concerns regarding her credibility and the fact that she had to testify in her husband's presence concerning facts involving him and his family. She did not have an opportunity to fully present her claim.
The RPD's conclusion is not correct. The RPD examined neither the female appellant's profile as a woman forced to live with her in-laws nor her marital situation.

I allow the female appellant's request, and her file is referred to a differently constituted panel for it to re-determine the female appellant's claim taking into account these reasons from the perspective of section 96. The children's claims
The RPD did not draw any specific conclusions regarding the children's claim since it determined that the appellants were not credible.
Based on the documentary evidence, in the event of separation, children generally go with their mother,8 as was also confirmed at the hearing.
Insofar as the minor appellants' claim is based on that of their mother, I allow their request and refer their files to the RPD for analysis concurrently with that of the female appellant.
I dismiss the appeal of XXXX XXXX and confirm the RPD's determination that he is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The appeals of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX are allowed. I refer the matter to the RPD with the following directions: DIRECTIONS FOR THE REFUGEE PROTECTION DIVISION

The matter shall be heard by a differently constituted panel for re-determination taking into account these reasons. The new panel and the interpreter must be female.
